title_original: Get me a 747 and deploy the oxygen masks! The British pilot behind Hollywood’s greatest inflight scenes
excerpt_original: An emergency landing for Bridesmaids, a humiliation for Ben Stiller in Focker-in-Law, a giant toilet for Britney Spears in the Toxic video … Richard Chan, No 1 provider of airplane cabin sets, recalls his finest work With Thanksgiving having just kicked off holiday season in the…

blocks.text: W ith Thanksgiving having just kicked off holiday season in the US, millions of people are boarding flights, many more concerned than ever about how chaotic that might be. Aside from the shock of the recent FAA shutdown , not a day seems to go by without a viral video of someone behaving badly or being removed from an airplane: Saturday Night Live even did a sketch about the introduction of a “new airline class” , with a whole section of a plane reserved for “crazy people”.

blocks.alt: Aero Mock-Ups’ warehouse in North Hollywood.
blocks.caption: Aero Mock-Ups’ warehouse in North Hollywood. Photograph: James Bartlett

blocks.text: In the big Thanksgiving movie Focker-In-Law , Ben Stiller has a lengthy and awkward encounter with a flight attendant who is summoned by a passenger called Olivia, played by Ariana Grande. On arrival, he learns that Olivia is his potential daughter-in-law and, of course, that means more trouble with his ex-CIA father-in-law Jack, played by Robert De Niro.

The SNL and Focker-in-Law scenes were shot on the ground in New York with the help of Aero Mock-Ups , a specialist airline interior prop and set warehouse based in Hollywood. The list of shows they’ve provided mid-air mock ups for is impressive: Grey’s Anatomy, Young Sheldon, Orange Is the New Black, Yellowjackets, Hacks, Westworld and Modern Family are among the series they’ve worked on.

In business for nearly 40 years, they have a base in New York, but boast the capability to ship their “Set-in-a-Box” (four portholes and a number of seats) anywhere across the US and Canada. Whether you need the first-class compartment of a 747, a Learjet cockpit, or a 40-foot section of wide (two aisle) or narrow (one aisle) body complete with seats, their three-man “ground crew” accesses their huge inventory and assembles it like a giant’s aviation Lego set.

If the cockpit’s buttons need to light up or oxygen masks deploy, they have that ready to go. They also have a large selection of “set dressing” such as uniforms, signs, lifejackets, name badges, coffee pots, blankets, headphones and even inflight snacks.

Run by British former pilot Richard Chan, the warehouse is also a treasure trove of airline and aviation history as it contains fuselage sections, seats and more from defunct airlines and aircraft. The first thing you see when you come into the office is a pair of seats from Concorde, which Chan admits is his favourite aviation possession, though he’s reluctant to name his most memorable project. “There’s about 600,” he says, “and my favourite is always the one I’m working on.”

blocks.alt: One of Aero Mock-Ups’s airplane interior sets.
blocks.caption: One of Aero Mock-Ups’ airplane interior sets. Photograph: James Bartlett

blocks.text: When pressed, Chan admits that he often points out the oversized airplane toilet they constructed for the Toxic video by Britney Spears as a highlight. As well as TV shows and pop videos, the company’s credit list also includes blockbuster movies such as The Avengers, Transformers: Dark of the Moon, Spider-Man: Homecoming, Inception, The Bourne Ultimatum, Furious 7 and F9, Argo, and Bridesmaids, which had an especially memorable airplane scene involving sedatives, hallucinations and an emergency landing.

Born in Elstree, Hertfordshire, to a Chinese father and a Belgian mother, Chan, 69, was raised and educated at private school in England. Despite being raised right under the flightpath of nearby Elstree Aerodrome, Chan didn’t originally have a plan to become a pilot: “After I did my O and A-levels, I looked into the careers room. The file of job choices was Accountant, Architect, and then Airline. I stopped there.”

blocks.alt: Richard Chan smiles while sitting in an aisle seat inside an aeroplane cabin mock-up
blocks.caption: ‘My favourite is always the one I’m working on’ … Richard Chan of Aero Mock-Ups. Photograph: James Bartlett

blocks.text: He soon realised that “planes are all made in America, fuel is cheaper there, and the weather sucks in Britain, so if I’m going to spend all that money to get a pilot’s licence, why don’t I go to Los Angeles? California was the centre of the aerospace industry, and Los Angeles has a very busy airspace. If I’m going to jump, why not jump into the deep end?”

While working towards his advanced flight training, he had what he calls an unscheduled landing. “I somewhat lost my nerve to fly and be responsible for the safety of 200-300 people every flight, simple as that,” he admits. “But I wanted to stay in aviation, so I went to work for cargo line Flying Tigers, and for an aviation parts company.”

Using his knowledge from working at a salvage company that aided the FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board in accident reconstruction, Chan was able to fully utilise his contacts for sourcing rare parts to sell on. “That’s where it started. And then when the internet arrived, I could contact people all over the world.”

One day, one of the operators in Honolulu, Hawaii, a regular stopover for the Flying Tigers, offered him a Boeing cabin interior that was being decommissioned. “I was going to strip it for parts, but my secretary at the time used to be a script supervisor, and she said she wanted to show it to some people. Soon after I had my first TV job: Nightmare on Elm Street: Freddy’s Nightmares. The second was sitcom Married … With Children, a scene when Al Bundy (played by Ed O’Neill) takes off his shoes when he’s on board, and the oxygen masks drop down!”

Sometimes Chan has had to travel to auctions or desert “bone yards”, and often when he bought, he bought big: everything in the interior, right down to the light bulbs. “You can’t pick and choose,” he says.

blocks.alt: Hanging restroom, gate, and flight destination signs displayed in a warehouse with wooden ceiling beams
blocks.caption: Where to next? … Aero Mock-Ups’ warehouse. Photograph: James Bartlett

blocks.text: Aside from entertainment, Aero Mock-Ups also works in the corporate arena. Post-9/11, Chan opened his doors to cabin crews looking for guidance about how to protect themselves and the passengers. Martial arts, special forces and law enforcement teams all came to demonstrate tactics and establish new protocols.

Chan has a passion to make all air travel a safe and comfortable experience, and his company assembled the Cabin Experience, part of the Sensory Room at Terminal 1 of the San Francisco international airport. The room is a safe place for neurodivergent travellers, but also those who are anxious about flying or are new passengers who want to know what to expect. “We’re working on another room for Terminal 3, and this one will have live electrics,” he says.

Chan leads me on a tour of the warehouses and their mind-boggling selection of airline and aviation materials. To see these items out of context and all together – to say nothing of walking down the aisles of empty planes indistinguishable from the real thing – is almost a liminal experience, like you’ve stepped into the Backrooms .

In recent years Chan has backed off buying more aircraft interiors. He reaches for his smartphone and pulls up images of airplanes, active and prototype, that are electric or even hydrogen-powered. “That’s the future, and they look like something from out of Thunderbirds!”

He’s even thinking of selling off some of his vintage airline material, much of which is now highly collectible. Even so, Chan can’t see himself retiring soon. “I’m still here six days a week,” he says.

His plan for the next year or so is to turn the warehouses into a complete, on-site airport set experience, allowing filming to go through the airport and on to the plane. Actors would enter via the check-in desk, pass through a TSA screening machine and then go into a waiting room with seats and doors to other gates. It’s a surreal experience visiting Aero Mock Ups – it all feels incredibly familiar to be in this space, yet blissfully quiet and empty too. “If only real travel was like this,” laughs Chan.
